author: reek
body: The first-boot ceremony on the GOP framebuffer (B2.2 + B2.3). The flow mirrors FirstBoot's phase model -- welcome, identity, upstream, complete -- rendered with GopDraw and driven by GopText fields over whichever keyboard the machine has: PS/2 by IRQ, or USB HID by the pump the context carries (wz-kbd), because on the Option A boot path firmware is gone: no ConOut, no ConIn, and on most modern machines no PS/2 controller either.

author: reek
body: Every waiting loop is a self-recursive act tail (constant stack under the compiler's TCO) whose idle path allocates nothing; the hosting program compiles with the pet flag like every boot-path poll loop.

author: reek
body: The wait polls through kbd-take so a USB keyboard's Enter arrives exactly like a PS/2 one; with no USB keyboard connected the pump is a flag test and this is gk-take in a loop, unchanged.

author: reek
body: This wait is also the keyboard proof gate, because it is the one place the boot stops and asks a human to press something. A key -- any key, not just the Enter this screen wants -- proves the keyboard delivers, and restarts the window. Silence proves nothing on its own: a machine whose keyboard is simply unattended looks exactly like a machine whose USB HID endpoint enumerated and never spoke. The gate treats them the same on purpose, because the remedy is harmless to the first and is the only remedy for the second: after a bounded silence the controller goes back to firmware (kbd-handback) and its legacy emulation answers instead. The cost is the USB boot stick, which shares the controller; a machine nobody can type on could not have used it anyway.

author: reek
body: Both clocks are reported on the glass while the gate waits, because a boot that fails to fire must say WHY: if pit stays 0 while rtc climbs, the timer interrupt is dead on that machine and everything else built on the tick (the watchdog, preemption, any timeout) is dead with it. That is a finding, not a nuisance.

author: reek
body: The gate fires at most once -- the handback records its own decision -- so a firmware that refuses to take the controller back is not asked twice.

author: reek
body: wz-wait-enter-from tail-calls ITSELF so the compiler's TCO turns the poll into a jump; the gate is a helper returning an integer, exactly as the menu's dispatchers are, because mutual recursion would grow the stack until the machine died waiting for a keystroke.

author: reek
body: The gate reports its own vitals when the second turns over, when a key arrives, and -- only on a machine whose clock has never moved at all -- on a spin interval. The first two builds of this gate each depended on a clock to say anything, and each went silent on the one machine it was written for: a screen that prints nothing cannot be distinguished from a loop that is not running, an RTC that never ticks, or a keyboard streaming garbage that resets the window every iteration. Those are three different faults and they looked identical. The third arm is what keeps that guarantee: the spin counter is the one number that cannot lie, and a clockless machine still gets a line.

author: reek
body: The spin backstop is for ONE case, and it must never pre-empt a working clock: a machine where neither the timer interrupt NOR the real-time clock advances at all. Written as a plain spin budget it fired within a second or two on real silicon -- that CPU spins tens of millions of times a second, so sixty million spins is not "a long wait", it is an instant -- and it handed the controller back before the thirty-second window had even begun, switching off the very keyboard pump whose silence it was supposed to be measuring. A budget in spins is not a duration. It only becomes one when there is nothing else to count by.

author: reek
body: The window is THIRTY seconds and it announces itself, because the handback is not free: it costs the USB stick, and on a machine whose firmware offers no legacy emulation it costs the USB keyboard too. A ten-second window fired while a human was still reading the welcome screen -- caught in the emulator, where the fallback has nothing to fall back TO, and a working keyboard was destroyed by the mechanism meant to save it. So the machine now says what it is about to do, counts down where the operator can see it, and any keystroke at all calls the whole thing off. A person who has not touched a key in half a minute, on a screen that says "Press Enter to begin", does not have a working keyboard.

author: reek
body: The clockless floor only. A machine whose RTC turns over repaints on the second and never reaches this.

author: reek
body: A status row is cleared across the WHOLE panel, not across the text column: these lines are longer than the ceremony's prose, and a clear sized to the column leaves the tail of the previous, longer line standing beside the new one.

author: reek
body: An unreadable second (-1) is carried through as no change at all: prev is left standing, elapsed does not move, and the loop simply asks again. A clock that cannot be read is not a clock that has ticked.

author: reek
body: The passphrase protects the private key. Two masked entries must match and reach four characters; a failed attempt redraws the screen with the reason and starts over -- the retry is a tail self-call, so a stubborn typist costs no stack.

author: reek
body: Only ever write to the disk we booted from. The AHCI driver picks the first SATA disk it finds, which on a real machine with internal drives is NOT the boot medium -- so an unguarded write could land on the wrong disk. The boot medium is the one carrying our own CODEX.CDX; if the mounted volume has no CODEX.CDX, decline rather than risk another disk. (On real hardware the boot stick is USB mass storage, which these AHCI/IDE drivers cannot reach at all -- so the mount fails first and this guard is belt-and-suspenders until the USB stack lands.)

author: reek
body: Boot-diag trace lines (temporary, real-hardware bring-up): same bottom-region geometry as GopBoot's boot-trace, rows 4 and up, so on a machine with no serial the last line standing names the wizard step that died. Each screen's clear wipes them; a death mid-clear leaves them readable below the partial fill.
